messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 66
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Retail Worker
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 63

Mrs. Meera Kapoor sits in the chair across from me, her hands folded tightly in her lap, the knuckles white against the deep maroon of her sari. She is a small woman, sixty-six years old, with silver-streaked hair pulled back into a neat bun. She has been a widow for eleven years, and for the last eight of those, she has worked the evening shift at a discount department store in a strip mall, folding towels and stocking shelves. She tells me this with a kind of flat pride—she has never missed a shift, never called in sick. But lately, she says, she has been late. Twice this month. And that is not like her.

The story she tells begins on a Tuesday evening in late October, six months ago. She had closed the store at ten, as usual, and walked to her car in the employee lot at the back of the building. The lot is poorly lit, and she had mentioned this to her manager once, but nothing had changed. That night, a man was waiting near her car. She did not see him until she was unlocking the door. He was young, she thinks, though she cannot remember his face. She remembers the weight of him, the smell of cigarettes and sweat, the way her keys clattered on the asphalt. She remembers the gravel digging into her back. She remembers thinking, *If I scream, no one will hear me.* She did not scream.

For the first few weeks after, she told no one. She went to work the next day, moved through the motions—folding, stacking, greeting customers with a practiced, polite smile. She told herself it was over, that she was fine. But the nights became unbearable. She stopped sleeping in her bedroom, where the windows face the street. Instead, she sleeps on the floor of her daughter’s old room, a room with no windows at all, a narrow closet of a space. She brings a pillow and a blanket and lies on the carpet, her back pressed against the wall. She does not undress. She wears her work clothes, even to sleep, so that if she has to run, she is ready.

She has stopped eating dinner. She used to enjoy cooking—simple South Asian meals, dal and rice, a vegetable curry—but now the smell of food makes her nauseous. She drinks tea, black, and that is all. She has lost weight, though she does not notice it. Her daughter, who lives two hours away, called last week and said, “Amma, you sound different.” Mrs. Kapoor told her she was tired. She does not want her daughter to worry. She does not want anyone to know.

At work, she has become vigilant. She scans every male customer who enters the store, watching their hands, their eyes. She avoids the back aisle, where the stockroom door is. She asks her coworkers to walk her to her car, but she never tells them why. She says it is because she is old, because her eyesight is bad at night. They believe her.

She has also stopped praying. This is the detail that seems to trouble her most. She was raised Hindu, and for decades she maintained a small altar in her living room, with a picture of Ganesh and a brass lamp she would light each morning. She has not lit the lamp in five months. She says she cannot bring herself to kneel. The posture, she explains—the bowing of the head, the closing of the eyes—feels too vulnerable. She cannot be in a position where she cannot see what is coming.

When she speaks of the assault, her voice does not waver. She uses clinical words, as though she is describing something that happened to someone else. But her hands remain folded, white-knuckled, and her gaze stays fixed on a point just past my shoulder. She does not cry. She tells me she has not cried since it happened. She says she is afraid that if she starts, she will not stop, and she cannot afford that. She has a shift tomorrow. The towels need to be folded. The store opens at nine.
